## getting_started/about.md

title: About mp-units
summary: mp-units is a modern C++ library for compile‑time dimensional analysis and unit/quantity manipulation. The earliest versions were inspired by `std::chrono::duration`, but with each release the interfaces intentionally diverged to provide a better user experience.

title: Decompose a Vector Quantity into Components

## how_to_guides/advanced_usage/photometric_conditions.md

title: Working with Photometric Conditions
summary: Photometric quantities weighted with different spectral sensitivity functions (photopic, scotopic, mesopic, or custom ones) share the same units but must never be added, compared, or converted to each other. mp-units keeps each photometric condition in its own quantity hierarchy, so mixing them does not compile. The rationale and the full description of the model live in the ISQ user's guide.
code: `quantity` 20, `si::lumen_of` 11, `isq::scotopic_vision` 8, `si::lumen` 8, `QuantityOf` 5, `isq::photopic_vision` 5, `si::watt` 4, `si::lux_of` 3, `isq::photometric_condition_base` 2, `one` 2, `si::candela_of` 2, `si::lux` 2, `si::metre` 2, `dimensionless` 1, `isq::mesopic_vision` 1, `si::candela` 1

## how_to_guides/advanced_usage/polar_and_spherical_coordinates.md

title: Working with Polar and Spherical Coordinates
summary: The built-in `cartesian_vector` is the representation the library uses for vector quantities, and all vector arithmetic happens in Cartesian components. Many problems, though, are stated in polar or spherical coordinates: a radar contact at a range and a bearing, a launch velocity given as a speed and two angles, a joystick deflection as a magnitude and a direction.

## how_to_guides/advanced_usage/pure_dimensional_analysis.md

title: Pure Dimensional Analysis
summary: This guide shows you how to use mp-units for pure dimensional analysis—working with dimensions and quantity specifications without actual numerical values. You'll learn how to embed dimensions into custom types, validate dimensional consistency at compile-time, and build sophisticated systems like symbolic computation or automatic differentiation while maintaining full dimensional correctness.

## how_to_guides/advanced_usage/tensor_representation_of_axial_vectors.md

title: Represent an Axial Vector as an Antisymmetric Tensor
summary: This guide shows how to work with a quantity, such as angular velocity, that the ISQ defines as a vector but that your domain represents as an antisymmetric tensor (a skew-symmetric matrix). ## how_to_guides/advanced_usage/working_with_measurement_uncertainty.md

## users_guide/advanced_topics/quantity_spec_conversions.md

title: Quantity Specification Conversions
summary: Every time a quantity is copied into a differently typed one, passed through the call operator of a quantity specification, or put through `quantity_cast`, the library has to answer one question: how are these two quantity specifications related? The answer decides whether the code compiles as written, needs an explicit conversion, needs a cast, or is rejected altogether.

## users_guide/advanced_topics/representation_types.md

## users_guide/framework_basics/character_of_a_quantity.md

title: Character of a Quantity
summary: A quantity's character has two orthogonal axes: its tensor order (scalar, vector, or tensor) and its numeric field (real or complex). The two are independent, so every combination is possible: a velocity is a real vector, a voltage phasor a complex scalar, and a complex field amplitude in electromagnetics a complex vector.

## users_guide/systems/cgs.md

title: Centimetre-Gram-Second (CGS) System
summary: The Centimetre-Gram-Second (CGS) system is a metric system of physical units based on the centimetre, gram, and second as base units. It was widely used before the adoption of the SI system and is still employed in certain scientific fields, particularly in theoretical physics, astronomy, and some areas of chemistry.

## workshops/extensions/custom_quantity_specifications.md

title: Custom Quantity Specifications
summary: While the ISQ (International System of Quantities) provides many standard quantity types, real-world applications often require domain-specific distinctions between quantities that share the same dimension. For example, in an elevator system, both cabin mass and passenger mass are masses (kg), but treating them as interchangeable could lead to incorrect calculations or unsafe designs.
